2.17.m: Somaśarmā said: / O goddess, all the excellent establishment of dharma has been fully related. / How might I obtain a son who is all-knowing and endowed with virtues?
Tell me, O highly fortunate one, if you know, O lady of good vows; / charity, dharma, and the like [bear fruit] in the hereafter and here, without doubt.
Sumanā said: / Go to Vasiṣṭha, who knows dharma, and pray to that great sage; / from him you will surely obtain a son who knows dharma and is fond of dharma.
Sūta said: / When this speech was spoken by her, Somaśarmā, the best of Brahmins, [said]: / 'I will do thus, O auspicious lady, according to your word, without doubt.'
Having spoken thus, Somaśarmā, the best of Brahmins, went swiftly / to Vasiṣṭha, the knower of all, divine, the best among ascetics,
standing on the bank of the Gaṅgā, holy, residing in his hermitage, the best of Brahmins, / surrounded by blazing splendor, like a second sun,
shining, great-souled, devoted to the sacred, the best of Brahmins. / Bowing with devotion to the lord of Brahmins like a staff, again and again,
the sinless son of Brahmā, of great splendor, spoke to him: / 'Sit down on a sacred seat with ease, O very intelligent one.'
Having spoken thus, that lord of yogins spoke again to the ascetic: / 'In your house, among your sons, my child, your wife, and your servants, is there always
welfare, O highly fortunate one, and in your meritorious rites and sacred fires? / Are you free from disease in your limbs, and do you always preserve dharma?'
Having spoken thus, the very wise one spoke again to Suśarmā: / 'What pleasing deed may I do, very agreeable to you, O best of Brahmins?'
Having thus addressed the Brahmin, that jar-born sage paused, / when that was spoken by the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha, the eminent sage.
He spoke to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, best among ascetics: / 'O lord, please listen to my words with a deeply gracious mind.
If you are to do me a great favour, O foremost among sages, / then dispel the doubt of my inquiry, O best of the twice-born.
By what sin has this poverty come, and why is there no joy from sons? / Resolve this doubt of mine, dear sir; tell me from what sin it arises.
Bewildered by great delusion, I was awakened by my beloved wife, O twice-born one. / Sent by her, distressed, I have come to your presence, dear sir.
Explain all that, which destroys all doubt; / become the giver of liberation for me from the bond of worldly existence.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'Sons, friends, brothers, and other kinsmen and relatives— / these come to be for a man through five distinct divisions.
Those were indeed told to you earlier in your presence by Sumanā; / they are all bound by debt, they are bad sons, O best of the twice-born.
I shall explain before you the meritorious characteristic of a son: / one whose self is attached to merit, who is always devoted to truth and dharma,
endowed with purity and higher knowledge, an ascetic, foremost among the eloquent, / steadfast in all deeds, dedicated to the study of the Vedas,
a knower of all scriptures, a worshipper of gods and brāhmaṇas, / a performer of all sacrifices, generous, renounced, pleasant of speech,
always devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu, calm, self-controlled, always a good friend, / constantly devoted to his father and mother, affectionate to all his kinsmen,
a saviour of his lineage, learned, a sustainer of his family— / endowed with such virtues, he is a son who brings happiness.
Others are merely bound by connection, givers of grief and torment. / What purpose is served by such a one who is devoid of fruit?
They come and go, all of them, having inflicted terrible torment; / in the form of sons they all appear in worldly existence, O best of the twice-born.
The merit done in a previous life that was maintained by you— / I shall tell you all of that; listen once more to this wonder.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'In your previous birth, O very wise one, you were indeed a śūdra, not otherwise; / a farmer, devoid of knowledge, filled with great greed.
Having one wife, always hostile, having many sons, never giving; / you did not know dharma, nor did you listen to truth.
No gift was given by you, no scripture listened to; / nor did you ever make a pilgrimage to a sacred ford, O noble-minded one.
Thus the way of agriculture was pursued by you again and again, O twice-born one; / the rearing of animals and cattle, O best of the twice-born,
and the repeated keeping of buffaloes and horses; / such was the work previously done by you, O best of the twice-born.
And abundant wealth was likewise amassed through greed; / yet its expenditure was never made by you on anything truly virtuous.
A gift was not given to a worthy recipient; even seeing a weak man, / no wealth was given by you out of compassion.
Cattle, buffaloes, and the rest—all livestock was accumulated by you; / and selling them, O twice-born one, vast wealth was hoarded by you.
Having sold buttermilk, clarified butter, and milk, and then curd, / you contemplated famine, O twice-born one, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu.
Grain was made truly expensive here by you, O best of brāhmaṇas; / being merciless, a gift was never given by you at any time.
Worship of the gods was never performed by you, O twice-born one; / even when holy festival days arrived, wealth was not given to the brāhmaṇas.
When the time for ancestral rites arrived, it was not performed by you with faith; / your virtuous wife would say, "This day has arrived,
the time for the ancestral rites of your father-in-law and mother-in-law, O noble-minded one." / Hearing that word of hers, you would flee, abandoning your home.
The path of dharma was never seen by you, nor ever heard by you; / greed was your mother, father, brother; greed was your kinsmen and relatives.
Greed alone was cherished, having always abandoned dharma; / therefore you have become sorrowful, severely afflicted by poverty.
Day after day great thirst increased in your heart; / whenever wealth in your house grew,
being burned by that thirst which had the form of fire, / even while sleeping well at night, you pondered anxiously:
"When day comes, I am always seized by great delusions: / when will a thousand, a hundred thousand, a crore, or ten million be mine?
When will a hundred billion, or a trillion, be in my house?" / Thus, though a thousand, a hundred thousand, a crore, and ten million,
a hundred billion, and a trillion came to be, the thirst never departs; / rather than leaving your body, it continually increases.
Nothing was ever given, offered into fire, or enjoyed by you, O twice-born one; / dug into the ground, it was hidden away, and your sons did not know of it.
You constantly adopted other means for the sake of the arrival of wealth, O twice-born; / wise as you were, you questioned people.
Asking about magical spades, salves, transmutation, and alchemy beyond that, / you wandered alone, utterly deluded by craving.
You constantly pondered the philosopher's stone and recipes granting magical success; / contemplating entry into subterranean cavities, you questioned eagerly.
Consumed by the fire of thirst, you found no happiness; / blazed by the fire of thirst, you cried "Alas, alas!", deprived of sense.
Thus deluded, O chief of twice-borns, you came under the sway of death; / even when your wife and sons inquired about that wealth,
the truth was never told by you; having abandoned your life-breaths, you went to Yama. / Thus your whole past account has been related by me.
By this action, O twice-born, you have become destitute and poor. / In this world, the one whose sons are good, always possessing devotion,
virtuous, endowed with knowledge, and always devoted to truth and dharma, / are born in his house when Viṣṇu is pleased with him.
Wealth, grain, a wife, and endless sons and grandsons / he enjoys in the mortal world, when Viṣṇu is gracious to him.
Without the grace of Viṣṇu, one cannot obtain wife and sons, / nor a good birth and noble family, O twice-born one, [which lead to] that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.'

2.18.m: Somaśarman said: / 'The sin committed in my previous birth has been recounted to me by you, O sage; / but that state of being a śūdra was abandoned by me, O chief of the twice-born.
How then was the status of a Brahmin attained by me, O best of the twice-born? / Tell me the entire cause of that, O scholar learned in theoretical and experiential wisdom!
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'Whatever deed based on dharma was undertaken by you previously, O twice-born one, / that I shall declare; listen, if you please.
A certain sinless brāhmaṇa, of virtuous conduct, very learned, / a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous in soul, was ever intent upon Viṣṇu.
Under the guise of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, he wandered alone over the earth; / wandering about, that high-minded one came to your house.
He requested a single place to dwell, O best of the twice-born; / and it was granted by your wife, and by you together with your sons.
"Come, come, O holy brāhmaṇa, comfortably into my good house!" / Thus you said repeatedly to that pure Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa.'

"Stay here comfortably, O one of good vows; this house is yours.
Today I am blessed; today I have gone to a sacred pilgrimage place.

Today the fruit of a pilgrimage has been attained from seeing your pair of feet."
A holy and excellent cow-shed was offered [to him] for lodging.

Having massaged his limbs and rubbed his feet,
and washed them with water, he bathed in the water from his feet.

You offered fresh ghee, curd, milk, food, and buttermilk
to that very brāhmaṇa, the great-souled one.

In this way the twice-born sage was satisfied by you, together with your wife
and your sons, O highly fortunate one—a Vaiṣṇava learned in knowledge.

Then, when morning arrived on an auspicious, fortune-giving day,
the sin-destroying Ekādaśī of the bright half of Āṣāḍha,

arrived on that day, destroying all sins,
on which the god Hṛṣīkeśa enters the sleep of yoga.

Reaching that [day], the people, wise with understanding, abandoned
all household tasks, intent on meditation on Viṣṇu, O twice-born.

They made a great festival with songs and auspicious instrumental music;
all the brāhmaṇas praised [him] with the Vedas and auspicious hymns.

Having reached such a great festival, that best of brāhmaṇas
remained there on that day; fasting took place.

The glorification of Ekādaśī was recited by the brāhmaṇa;
together with his wife and sons, he heard the unsurpassed dharma.

When that great holiness was heard, [you were] urged by your wife and sons:
"Through association with this twice-born, observe this vow."

Having heard that great speech giving all religious merit,
with a resolved mind: "I will observe this vow,"

going with your wife and sons, a bath in the river was performed by you;
with a joyful heart, O twice-born, Madhusūdana was worshipped

with all sacred offerings, and with perfumes, incenses, and the like,
keeping a vigil at night with dances, songs, and so forth.

In the company of the brāhmaṇa, bathing in the river was done again;
the lord of the gods was worshipped with auspicious flowers, incenses, and the like.

Bowing with devotion to Govinda and bathing him again and again,
such an offering was given to the great-souled brāhmaṇa.

Bowing to that twice-born with devotion, a good sacrificial gift was given to him;
he broke the fast, O twice-born, together with his sons, wife, and others.

He was sent off by you alone with devotion and good intent;
thus this vow was observed by you, O best of the twice-born.

Through association with that brāhmaṇa and by the grace of Viṣṇu,
you attained the status of a brāhmaṇa, endowed with true dharma.

By the power of that vow, a noble family was attained by you,
of brāhmaṇas, highly wise, endowed with true dharma.

To that very brāhmaṇa, the great-souled Vaiṣṇava,
well-prepared food was given with faith and true disposition.

By the power of that gift, sweet food is available [to you];
yet you were bewildered by great delusions, and your mind was filled with thirst.

In your previous birth, O twice-born, wealth alone was amassed;
it was not given by you to brāhmaṇas, or to the poor and others,

as you were dying out of greed for your wife and sons.
By the effect of that sin, poverty entered you.

Having completely cast off greed for a son and rejected affection far away,
you became sonless as the fruit of that very sin.

A good son and family, O twice-born, wealth, grain, excellent women,
a good birth and a good death, good enjoyments and happiness,

kingship, heaven, and liberation, whatever is difficult to obtain,
[come] through the grace of that god, the great-souled Viṣṇu.

Therefore, having worshipped Govinda, the healthy Nārāyaṇa,
you will reach that highest abode, the supreme step of Viṣṇu.

Good sons, wealth, grain, good enjoyments, and happiness—
all your past actions performed in the previous birth,

that has been fully recounted by me before you, O twice-born.
Knowing this, O fortunate one, be devoted to Nārāyaṇa."

Enlightened indeed by the son of Brahmā, that eminent twice-born of great majesty,
filled with joy, having bowed down with devotion to Vasiṣṭha there,

taking leave of the twice-born, went home, joyful on reaching his well-disposed wife:
"All the past deeds of mine were revealed by that very twice-born, through your favor,

O noble lady, brought to light by Vasiṣṭha; today my delusion has been destroyed.
I shall worship Madhusūdana; I shall go to liberation, that supreme step."

Having heard this supreme, great speech, highly auspicious and truly granting auspiciousness, / filled with joy, she said to her beloved: 'You are meritorious; you have been enlightened by the brahmin.'

2.19.m: Sūta said: / The most wise Somaśarman, the best among men, together with Sumanā, / went to the auspicious confluence of the Kapilā on the bank of the Revā, which grants great merit.
Having bathed there, the wise man, offering libations to the gods and ancestors, / performed austerity with an entirely tranquil mind, murmuring [the name of] auspicious Nārāyaṇa.
Joined in meditation through the twelve-syllable mantra, the high-minded man of firm vows / [meditated] on that very god of gods, Vāsudeva.
While sitting, lying down, moving, and in dreams, he beheld Keśava, / always remaining steady, freed from desire and anger.
And that virtuous, fortunate woman, devoted to her husband, / Sumanā, served her beloved who was endowed with austerity.
While he was meditating, fear was displayed to him by obstacles; / black serpents fierce with poison approached that great-souled man.
Beside that Somaśarman as he practiced austerities, / seen lions, tigers, and elephants brought about terrible fear.
Vetālas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and fierce Pretas / displayed terrifying, life-destroying fear.
Various immensely terrifying lions assembled there; / their mouths formidable with fangs, they roared most dreadfully.
From the meditation on Viṣṇu, that righteous-minded, wise man did not swerve, / nor was that best of sages shaken by the deep-rooted, great obstacles.
Thus the best of brahmins, Somaśarman, did not waver from his meditation, / though severely afflicted by howling windstorms, cold, and heavy rain.
A lion arrived there, most terrifying with a roaring sound; / seeing it, terrified with fear, the brahmin remembered Nṛhari:
Resembling sapphire, clad in yellow garments, endowed with great splendor, / the god bearing the conch and discus, holding the mace and lotus,
with a great pearl necklace imitating the luster of the moon, / radiant also with the Kaustubha gem—Janārdana,
whose chest shines with the divine mark of Śrīvatsa, / his limbs adorned with every ornament, his eyes resembling a hundred-petaled lotus,
with a gently smiling face, fully gracious, adorned with garlands of gems, / gleaming Hṛṣīkeśa—unwavering meditation was performed by him [saying]:
'You alone are my refuge, Kṛṣṇa, compassionate to those seeking refuge; / homage be to the god of gods! What can cause me fear?
Within the belly of which great soul are the three worlds and the seven others— / I have entered his refuge; where indeed can fear be for me?
From fear of whom the immensely powerful Kṛtyās and other [spirits] depart— / in him, the destroyer of all fear, have I taken refuge.
The great terror of all sins and of the Dānavas, / the protector of the devotees of Viṣṇu—in him have I taken refuge.
Of all the gods and the high-souled Dānavas, / he who is the refuge of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa—in him have I taken refuge.
The fearless one, for the destruction of fear, possessed of knowledge for the destruction of sin, / and the sole one in the form of Indra—in him have I taken refuge.
The destroyer of diseases, who has the nature of medicine, / free from illness and free from transient joy—in him have I taken refuge.
Immovable, he moves the worlds, free from sin, and knowledge itself; / having taken refuge in him, what will fear do to me?
The protector of all the virtuous, who is free from sickness, / who protects the universe, the Self of the universe—in him have I taken refuge.
He who in the form of the king of beasts shows fear before me— / having taken refuge in him, I bow down to Narasiṃha.
A wild elephant, intoxicated with rut and huge in body, has arrived; / the god whose gait is sportive as an elephant, affectionate to those seeking refuge,
who has an elephant face, endowed with knowledge, holding a noose and a goad, / whose mouth is Death, elephant-trunked—I have thoroughly taken refuge in him.
The striker of Hiraṇyākṣa, the Boar—in him have I taken refuge; / to Vāmana I surrender, affectionate to those seeking refuge.
Short ones, dwarfs, hunchbacks, Pretas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and others, / all wearing the form of death, show fear to me.
I have surrendered to the immortal one; what will fear do to me? / The friend of brahmins, the giver of Brahman, Brahmā, Hari consisting of knowledge of Brahman—
to him have I surrendered for refuge; what will fear do to me? / He who is fearlessness to the world, destroyer of fear, and creator of fear—
to him who takes the form of fear have I surrendered; what will fear do to me? / The savior of all worlds, the destroyer of all sinners,
in him, Janārdana who is the form of dharma, have I taken refuge. / He who assumes a wonderful form in battle to protect the gods—
I will go to his refuge; he is my perpetual resort. / The storm wind is exceedingly violent; my body suffers greatly.
To him have I surrendered for refuge; he is my perpetual resort. / Extreme cold, torrential rain, and heat causing torment—
in that god who is in the form of these have I taken refuge. / These fearful agitators of mine have arrived in the form of Time;
in them, who are always the manifestations of Hari, have I taken refuge.
Whom as the god of all, the Supreme Lord, pure and isolated, a lamp consisting of knowledge, / they call Nārāyaṇa, the eternally realized, Lord of the Siddhas—to him I surrender for refuge.'
Thus meditating and constantly praising Keśava, the destroyer of distress, / Hari was brought by him with devotion into his own heart at that moment.
Beholding that effort and courage of Somaśarman, / Hṛṣīkeśa, having manifested himself, said to him joyfully:
'O Somaśarman of great wisdom, listen together with your wife! / I am Vāsudeva, best of brahmins; ask for a boon, O you of noble vows!'
Addressed by him, that best of brahmins, opening both his eyes / and seeing the Lord of the universe, dark as a storm cloud, of great majesty,
his limbs adorned with all ornaments, equipped with all weapons, / endowed with divine marks, his eyes resembling the white lotus,
clad in yellow garments, radiant, the Lord of gods, / mounted upon the son of Vinatā, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
the true benefactor of Brahmā and others, of glorious fame in this universe, / always beyond this universe, beyond form, the teacher of the world—
filled with great joy, falling down prostrate like a staff before him / who was accompanied by Śrī, radiant, with the splendor of ten million suns,
joining his hands in supplication together with Sumanā, / said to him, 'Victory, victory! Victory, O Mādhava, giver of honor!
Victory, O Lord of Yogins, Indra among yogins! Victory, O you who recline upon the body of the serpent! / O limb of the sacrifice, victory, O Lord of sacrifice! Victory, O eternal, all-pervading one!
Victory, O Lord of all, infinite one, embodiment of sacrifice, homage be to you! / Victory, O foremost of the wise! Victory to you, leader of knowledge!
Victory, O giver of all, omniscient one! Victory to you, creator of all! / Victory, O Lord whose form is the soul! O great life, homage be to you!
Victory, O giver of wisdom, whose limbs are wisdom! Victory, O giver of life-breath! / Victory, O destroyer of sin, Lord of merit! Victory, O Master of merit, Hari!
Victory, O Lord whose essence is knowledge! Homage to you who are reachable by knowledge! / Victory, O lotus-petal-eyed one! Homage to you who have a lotus at the navel!
Victory, O Govinda, Gopāla! Victory, O conch-bearing, stainless one! / Victory, O discus-bearer, unmanifest one! Homage to you whose form is manifest!'

[He prayed:] "Victory to the one whose limbs shine with valor, victory to the lord of valor!
Victory to the one whose body delights in Lakṣmī; homage to you who are composed of the Vedas!

Victory to the one whose limbs shine with valor, victory to the giver of exertion!
Victory to exertion and to time; homage, homage to exertion!

Victory to the one capable of effort, the sustainer of the three exertions;
homage to you, that dharma who sets exertion in battle into motion!

Homage to the golden-seeded one; homage to you, that radiance,
to the one whose nature is supreme radiance, and who consists of all radiance!

To the destroyer of the radiance of Daityas, and the remover of the radiance of sins,
for the benefit of cows and brāhmaṇas, homage to the Supreme Self!

Homage to the enjoyer of oblations, and homage to you who carry the havis!
Homage indeed to the bearer of the kavya, homage to you whose form is svadhā!

To the sacrifice whose form is svāhā, to the purifier, homage, homage!
Homage to you who hold the bow Śārṅga, to Hari, the remover of sin!

To the impeller of the existent and the nonexistent, homage to the possessor of discernment!
Homage to the embodiment of the Vedas, to the purifier, homage, homage!

Homage to Harikeśa, to you the remover of all afflictions,
to Keśava, the supreme; homage to you, the supporter of the universe!

Homage to the maker of compassion, homage to you full of joy;
homage eternally to Ananta, the pure, the destroyer of affliction!

Homage eternally to bliss, to the pure, to the absolute one;
to you whose feet are bowed to by the Rudras, bowed to by Virañci!

Homage to you whose lotus-feet are bowed to by the lords of gods and asuras!
Homage, homage to the supreme lord, the unconquered, whose self is nectar!

Homage to the dweller in the milk ocean, to you who are dear to Padmā!
Homage, homage to the […] maker, to the pure, to the unmoving!

To the all-pervading and pervasive, the remover of all distress;
homage, homage to the Boar, homage to you the Great Tortoise!

Homage to the one whose form is Vāmana, to the great-souled Nṛsiṃha;
homage to the divine Rāma, and to the slayer of all kṣatriyas!

To the all-knowing Matsya, homage to you, Rāma!
Homage to Kṛṣṇa, to the Buddha; homage to the destroyer of mlecchas!

Homage to Kapila the twice-born, homage to you Hayagrīva!
Homage to the embodiment of Vyāsa, homage to you who consist of everything!"

Having thus praised Hṛṣīkeśa, he spoke to Janārdana:
"Even Brahmā does not know the furthest shore of your virtues, O purifier!

Nor is the all-knowing Rudra, nor the thousand-eyed one able to praise [you];
who indeed is able to speak? What kind of intellect is mine, O lord?

This hymn, without attributes or with attributes, was made by me to you, Keśava;
forgive my words and misspoken words; I am your servant, O one of good vows!
In birth after birth, O lord of the worlds, have mercy on me, O purifier!"

2.20.m:
Hari said:
By this penance, by this merit, by this truth, and also by this purifying hymn of praise, O twice-born one, / I am pleased. Choose a boon!
I grant a boon, O fortunate one, whatever is in your mind. / Whatever desire you wish, that I shall fulfill for you.

Somaśarman said:
First, grant me one coveted boon, O Kṛṣṇa, / with a very gracious mind, if there is truly mercy toward me:
Having obtained one birth after another, let me practice devotion to you. / Show me your supreme, unshakeable abode that grants liberation.
A son who delivers his lineage, endowed with divine marks, / constantly intent on devotion to Viṣṇu, the upholder of my lineage,
omniscient, all-giving, self-controlled, endowed with the splendor of penance, / ever a protector and worshiper of gods, brāhmaṇas, and the worlds,
a friend to the gods, meritorious in disposition, generous, learned in knowledge— / grant me such a son, and remove my poverty, O Keśava!

May it be so; there is no doubt. I choose this boon.
Hari said:
So be it, O best of the twice-born! It will come to pass, no doubt.
By my favor, an excellent son shall deliver your lineage. / You shall enjoy choice pleasures here, both divine and human,
witnessing supreme happiness, auspicious and born from having a son. / As long as you live, O brāhmaṇa, you shall not see sorrow.
You shall be a giver, an enjoyer, and an appreciator of virtue, without doubt; / and dying at a holy place, you shall go to the supreme state.
Having thus granted the boon to the twice-born and his beloved wife, Hari, / that god, disappeared, [vanishing] as if seen in a dream.
Then Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, accompanied by Sumanas, / at that sacred holy place on the bank of the Revā, which bestows great merit,
at Amarakaṇṭaka, that brāhmaṇa made meritorious gifts. / When a great deal of time had passed for that Somaśarman,
having bathed at the confluence of the Kapilā and the Revā, he stepped out; / and in front of him, the brāhmaṇa saw a white elephant,
brilliant, handsome, divine, full of spirit, with pleasing marks, / its body adorned with various ornaments, endowed with great splendor.
Its two temples were radiant with vermilion and saffron; / it was adorned with blue lotuses at its ears and equipped with flagstaffs.
Seated upon the elephant was a divine man, steadfast and very splendid, / endowed with divine marks and decorated with all kinds of ornaments,
wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrant pastes, / very gentle, full like the moon, accompanied by an umbrella and fly-whisks.
The virtuous one saw him again, mounted on the elephant and proceeding along, / praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas, exceedingly auspicious.
Having seen that handsome man endowed with divine marks together with the elephant, / Somaśarman reflected, his mind filled with wonder:
“Who is this divine-bodied one, observant of vows, going along having taken the road?” / While he was pondering thus, by the time he reached his house,
he saw that enchanting godlike figure entering the doorway of the house. / Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, was seized with great joy;
and that righteous-minded man hurried toward his own house. / But by the time he reached the door of the house, he did not see him at all.
That highly intelligent, best of the twice-born saw only flowers fallen, / delightful, divine, and fragrant, in his courtyard,
and smeared with sandal, holy saffron, and fragrant unguents; / he saw his own courtyard strewn with dūrvā grass and unbroken grains of rice.
Filled with wonder in this way, reflecting again and again, / the wise man saw Sumanas possessing divine and auspicious splendor.

Somaśarman said:
By whom were these divine ornaments given, / and the embellishment, beauty, good fortune, and adornments of clothing and jewelry?
Tell me the reason for that, O auspicious woman, without hesitation! / Having spoken thus to his wife, the best of the twice-born ceased.

Sumanas said:
Listen, beloved! Some supreme choice god arrived, / mounted on a white elephant and decorated with divine ornaments,
his limbs anointed with divine fragrance, endowed with divine wonders. / I do not know which god this was, served by brāhmaṇas and Gandharvas,
who arrived being praised by gods, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas. / Women rich in meritorious beauty, endowed with grace and embellishment,
abounding in the splendor of all ornaments, their every desire fulfilled— / together with them, before my eyes, by that noble man,
a square courtyard was filled with jewels, endowed with every beauty. / There, upon a sacred seat, I was indeed placed by the brāhmaṇas.
All of them gave me adornments of clothing and jewelry; / and with auspicious Vedic songs and meritorious songs from the scriptures,
I was consecrated by all of them; then they disappeared again. / All of them around me spoke to me once more, O best of the twice-born:
“We shall indeed all dwell in your house at all times. / Remain pure, O fortunate woman, always together with your husband!”

Having spoken thus, they all departed; such was what was seen by me.
Having heard that account which was told by her, the highly intelligent one
again fell into thought: “What is this that has been brought about by the divine?” / Then, having reflected, the highly intelligent Somaśarman,
dedicated to brāhmanical duties, observed the highest common religious duty. / From that fortunate man, she who was observant of vows conceived a child.
With that child in her womb, the lady shone even more brightly then, / endowed with a radiant son and possessed of the brilliance of a flame.
Through penance she gave birth to a son resembling a god. / Then the drums of the gods resounded in the sky;
the great gods blew conches, the Gandharvas sang charmingly, / and indeed all the Apsarases danced then.
Then Brahmā, accompanied by the gods, arrived, O best of the twice-born; / collected in mind, he gave him the name Suvrata.
Having bestowed the name, all the gods of great energy departed. / When those gods had departed, for his son
Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies. / When that fortunate son, Suvrata, fashioned by the gods, was born,
great prosperity, filled with wealth and grain, came to his house— / elephants, horses, buffaloes, cows, gold, and jewels.
Just as Kubera's abode shone with stores of wealth, / so too did that house of Somaśarman shine all around.
The best of the twice-born performed meditation, meritorious deeds, and other rites; / the brāhmaṇa went on pilgrimage to sacred sites, abounding in various merits.
Whatever other meritorious gifts there were, the best of the twice-born / gave there, intelligent and endowed with knowledge and merit.
Thus he achieved dharma and constantly maintained it. / The best of the twice-born performed the birth-rites and other rites for his son,
and had his marriage performed with great joy. / Sons endowed with virtues and marks were born to that son,
endowed with truth, dharma, and penance, and ever devoted to the dharma of giving gifts. / Somaśarman performed meritorious rites for them;
and the fortunate man rejoiced in the happiness of his grandsons. / Enjoying every comfort, he was free from old age and disease.
His body indeed was just like that of a twenty-five-year-old; / the wise Somaśarman shone like the brilliance of the sun.
And the blessed lady Sumanā also shone through her meritorious, auspicious deeds, / through her sons and grandsons, through gifts, vows, and restraints.
The large-eyed woman shone brilliantly through her meritorious deeds, such as devotion to her husband, / endowed with youth, as if sixteen years old.
The great-souled husband and wife, charming and auspicious, rejoiced, / endowed with joy, pure-minded, and blessed with great prosperity.
Thus of those two, endowed with virtuous conduct, was the life-story. / I shall now tell of the observance of vows of Suvrata, O best of the twice-born,
and how he properly worshipped the immaculate Nārāyaṇa.

2.21.m: Sūta said: / Once the divine Vyāsa, exceedingly amazed, / asked Brahmā, the lord of the universe, the whole story of Suvrata.
Vyāsa said: / O Soul of the world, O Arranger of the world, O God of gods, O great Lord, / I now desire to hear the deeds of Suvrata.
Brahmā said: / O son of Parāśara, O fortunate one, listen to the supreme, holy [story] / of the noble brahmin Suvrata, endowed with the practice of austerities.
The intelligent one named Suvrata meditated even from childhood; / while in the womb he had seen the god Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
From his practice in a previous life, he then entered into meditation on Hari, / on the god who holds the conch and discus, whose navel is a lotus, the giver of supreme merit.
He indeed meditated and reflected while singing, gaining knowledge, and reciting texts; / thus always meditating on the god Hari, the best of the twice-born
played in this way continually with children, the best among boys. / The boy's own name and those of the children he made the names of the great-souled Hari.
He, intelligent, pure-souled, and fond of virtue, did so; / the wise one would call his friend by the name of Hari:
“O Keśava, come, come! Come, O Mādhava, wielder of the discus! / Play with me; you are Puruṣottama himself!
Together we two must go forth, O Madhusūdana!” / Just so did the brahmin call out, using the names of Hari,
in playing, studying, laughing, lying down, singing, looking around, / in traveling, sitting, meditating, chanting mantras, gaining knowledge, and performing good deeds.
Thus he saw and thus he spoke of Janārdana, the Lord of the universe; / he meditated on him alone, the Lord of all, the great Lord.
In grass, wood, stone, dry things, and wet things, the righteous one / thus saw Keśava, lotus-eyed Govinda.
In the sky, on the earth, in mountains, and in forests, / in water, on land, in stone, and in living beings, the wise one,
the brahmin Suvrata, son of Sumanā, saw Nṛsiṃha. / Engaging in children's play, he delighted in this way day after day.
And with songs he sang of Kṛṣṇa in melodious rāgas with sweet syllables, / with rhythms accompanied by tempo, with melodious notes endowed with melodic lines.

Suvrata said: / “The knowers of the Veda constantly meditate on the enemy of demons, in whose body the entire universe resides. / I go for refuge to Madhusūdana, the master of yoga, who destroys all sins.
He who pervades all the worlds, and in whom all the worlds dwell, / to that Supreme Lord, devoid of all faults, I constantly bow down before his pair of feet.

Those whose minds are purified by Vedānta constantly recite [the praises of] Nārāyaṇa, the treasury of virtues, of infinite power; / to cross over the boundless, unfathomable, difficult ocean of cyclic existence, I take refuge entirely in him.

He is the royal swan upon the Mānasa lake of the minds of the lords of yogins; his pure power is indeed ever-present everywhere; / O enemy of the demons, protect me, a wretched soul, at your spotless and vast pair of feet!

I meditate on the god who is the master of all worlds, a moon right here to dispel the darkness of sorrow, / who has assumed dharma for the protection of the world, full of truth, the teacher of all worlds, the ruler of the gods.

With melodious songs and measures of rhythm, I sing incessantly of the one Śrīraṅga, the god of the world, / the spotless destroyer of ignorance, comparable to the sun, the source of all joy, endowed with greatness.

Thus, full of the nectar [of devotion], a treasury of the arts, I sing of his skill in song with unswerving devotions; / joined with the organs of his own yoga, having vision of the ultimate truth, he constantly sees the universe, moving and unmoving.
Whom the very sinful people here do not see at all, to that Keśava he constantly goes for refuge.”
Clapping his hands to keep the rhythm endowed with meter, / he sang of Kṛṣṇa in song and rejoiced with the boys.
Thus constantly devoted to play in the manner of a child, / Suvrata, the son of Sumanā, was devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu.
His mother said to the playing Suvrata, who possessed auspicious marks: / “Eat your meal, my child; hunger may torment you.”
The wise one spoke again to his mother Sumanā: / “I am truly satisfied with the great nectar, the essence of meditation on Hari.”
Sitting down upon the dining seat, he looked upon the sweet food: / “This food is Viṣṇu himself; the Self indeed depends upon food.
May Viṣṇu, who exists in the form of the Self, be satisfied with this food— / he whose abode is situated in the ocean of milk.
May Keśava attain satisfaction by this pure water, / by this betel, sandalwood paste, fragrant scents, and these delightful flowers.
Satisfied through the nature of his own Self, may Keśava attain satisfaction.” / When the righteous one went to his bed, he would then meditate on Kṛṣṇa:
“I have gone for refuge to Kṛṣṇa who is engaged in yogic sleep.” / Thus in food, clothing, sitting, and sleeping, the brahmin
would contemplate that Vāsudeva and offer everything to him. / Having reached youth, the righteous one abandoned sensual pleasures,
and engaged in meditation on Keśava on the excellent mountain Vaiḍūrya, / where there is the Siddheśvara liṅga, related to Viṣṇu and destroying sin.
And having meditated on the great Lord Rudra, named Oṃkāra, / the god magnified by Brahmā on the southern bank of the Narmadā,
taking refuge in Siddheśvara, he turned his mind toward austerity.

2.22.m: Vyāsa said: / O fortunate one, I shall now ask a question; tell me. / Earlier you spoke of Suvrata and the Lord,
how through past practice he meditated on the immaculate Nārāyaṇa. / In what family was Suvrata born in his previous birth?
Tell me that now: how was Hari worshipped / by him, O lord of gods? Who was this man laden with merit?
Brahmā said: / In the sacred city of Vaidiśa, filled with every prosperity, / there was a powerful king of great splendor, the son of Ṛtadhvaja.
His very wise son was known as Rukmabhūṣaṇa; / Saṃdhyāvalī was his lawful wife, illustrious and devoted to dharma.
Having begotten upon her a son resembling himself, / the prince then gave him the name Dharmāṅgada.

Endowed with all auspicious marks, devoted to his father,
that son of Rukmāṅgada was the foremost among the devotees of the Lord,

who, for his father's happiness, offered even his head to Mohinī.
By his Vaiṣṇava virtue and by devotion to his father,

Hṛṣīkeśa was exceedingly pleased with him. In bodily form, to Viṣṇu's abode
he was led—he who knew all dharmas, a Vaiṣṇava, foremost among the Sātvatas.

Dharmāṅgada was exceedingly wise, skilled in wisdom and knowledge.
Dwelling there, exceedingly wise, he was Dharma itself, an ornament of dharma,

rejoicing and enjoying divine pleasures that conformed to his desires.
When a thousand yugas had elapsed, Dharma, the ornament of dharma,

fell from that abode by the grace of Viṣṇu,
[and became] the wise [sage] named Suvrata, who increased the joy of Sumanā,

the son of Somaśarman, excellent, the foremost among the Lord's devotees.
The wise one performed austerity and became devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu.

Abandoning defects such as desire and anger, that best of twice-born,
restraining the assembly of the senses, practiced uninterrupted austerity.

On the excellent mountain Vaiḍūrya, near Siddheśvara,
he focused his mind and united it with Viṣṇu.

Remaining thus for a hundred years in meditation, of this great soul,
the Lord of the Universe, holding the conch, discus, and mace, became exceedingly pleased.

Keśava, together with Lakṣmī, granted him a supreme boon:
“O Suvrata of righteous soul! Awaken, O foremost among the wise!

Choose a boon; may you be blessed! I, Kṛṣṇa, have come to you.”
Having thus heard the unsurpassed words of Viṣṇu,

filled with immense joy upon seeing the god Janārdana,
he folded his hands in reverence and then bowed down.

When the great cloud of karma thunders, rains, and the lightning of my heaps of sins flashes,
my vision is lost in the screens of the darkness of delusion. To this wretched one, O Madhusūdana, give your hand!

The dense forest of worldly existence is crowded with many trees of sorrow and inhabited by lions of delusion;
it is ablaze with the fierce heat of fire; protect this one who is burning day and night, O Kṛṣṇa!

The tree of worldly existence here is very old yet tall, with delusion as its bulbous root and many sorrows as its branches;
it is laden with the foliage of attachment to wife and family, and it bears fruit, O Murāri; protect this fallen one who has climbed it, O Lord!

By the fires of sorrow with thick smoke of various delusions, and by griefs resembling death-inflicting separations,
I am burned, O Kṛṣṇa! Continually grant me liberation; anoint me always with the clouds of knowledge!

Into the veil of terrible darkness, the exceedingly deep pit named saṃsāra, I have fallen continually, O Kṛṣṇa;
you are truly merciful to me, who am wretched and terrified. Therefore, becoming detached, I have come to your refuge.

Those whose minds are disciplined and endowed with devotion, who meditate on you alone with an intellect of knowledge, attain your abode;
having bowed to your two exceedingly auspicious feet, upon which the hosts of gods and kinnaras meditate,

I speak of no other, I worship no other, I think of no other; I continually bow to the pair of your lotus feet.
Fulfill this desire of mine today, O Kṛṣṇa, so that my heaps of sins may depart far away.
O God, I am your servant, your attendant birth after birth; I continually remember the pair of your lotus feet.

If you are pleased, O Kṛṣṇa, grant me this boon, O Lord:
lead my mother and father in their bodily form to your abode, O Kṛṣṇa,

and myself too, O great God, along with me, without a doubt.”
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
“Thus shall your supreme purpose be accomplished, without a doubt.”

Hṛṣīkeśa, pleased with him and gratified by his devotion,
[led them both], and they went to the realm of Viṣṇu, free from burning and cosmic dissolution.

Both of them, Sumanā and Somaśarman, together with Suvrata,
until two kalpas had elapsed, that twice-born Suvrata

enjoyed, indeed enjoyed the divine worlds, O highly intelligent one!
Then, for the purpose of the work of the gods, into the house of Kaśyapa

the exceedingly wise one descended again by the word of that wielder of the discus,
who indeed enjoys the station of Indra by the grace of Viṣṇu.

Known as Vasudatta, bowed to by all the gods,
he indeed now enjoys the station of Indra as Vāsava in heaven.

All this has been narrated to you, the cause concerning creation.
Now I shall tell you something else, whatever you ask.”

Vyāsa said:
“The exceedingly wise Dharmāṅgada, the mighty son of Rukmāṅgada,
was born in the first Kṛta age at the time of creation as that Vāsava.

How then, O Lord of the god of gods, is there another Dharmāṅgada on earth,
another king Rukmāṅgada, and what is this lord of the thirty [gods]?

This doubt has arisen in me; you ought to explain that.”
Brahmā said:
“Come, I shall tell you what will destroy all your doubts.

It is the play of the Lord for the sake of creation, O best of the twice-born!
Just as days, fortnights, months, and seasons,

and years and Manus, so do the yugas return again.
Afterward, a kalpa comes, and thus I go to Janārdana.

I myself, O exceedingly wise one, and the moving and unmoving beings merge into me;
then he whose self is yoga creates the universe again just as before.

Again there am I, again the Vedas, again those deities and twice-born,
and likewise all those kings, adorned with their respective deeds,

come into being, O fortunate one; the wise man is not bewildered therein.
Just as the fortunate king Rukmāṅgada was in a previous kalpa,

so was this famous twice-born Dharmāṅgada born.
The exceedingly wise Rāma and others, and likewise Yayāti and Nahuṣa,

Manu and other great souls come into being and dissolve,
and kings devoted to righteousness enjoy the station of Indra.

Just as the heroic Dharmāṅgada enjoys that great station,
so too the Vedas, the gods, the Purāṇas along with the smṛtis.

All this has indeed been told before you, O best of the twice-born,
as well as the holy story of Suvrata that bestows a good destination.
Now I declare the unmanifest before you, O fortunate one.”

2.23.m:
The sages said:
“Wondrous is this auspicious story, conferring fortune and fame,
declared by you as destroying all sins, O foremost of speakers!

You ought to tell us this which pertains to creation,
how the creation was formerly in detail, O son of Sūta!”

Sūta said:
“I shall explain in detail the cause of creation and destruction,
by the mere hearing of which a person may attain omniscience.

The three worlds were pervaded even by Hiraṇyakaśipu;
having propitiated Brahmā through austerity, he obtained a very rare boon.

From that god, O fortunate ones, he obtained immortality as well;
pervading the worlds of the gods, he acquired lordship by himself.
Then the gods along with the gandharvas, the sages who had crossed to the other side of the Vedas, / the nāgas, the kinnaras, the siddhas, the yakṣas, and others as well,
placing Brahmā at their head, went to Lord Nārāyaṇa, / the Lord who was asleep upon the Ocean of Milk, having entered yogic sleep.
Having awakened him with great hymns of praise, the gods, with joined palms, / when the Lord of gods had awakened, the conduct of that wicked-minded one
they related, O very wise one. Having heard this, the Lord of the universe, / assuming the form of the Man-Lion, slew Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Again, in the form of the Boar, Hiraṇyākṣa of great strength [was slain]; / the holy earth was lifted up, and that asura was killed at that time.
And he caused other dānavas of terrible appearance to be killed. / When these great dānavas had thus been destroyed,
and those other sons of Diti were indeed destroyed at that time, / and the gods had regained their stations, great as they were,
and sacrifices indeed commenced, along with all dharmic acts, / and all the worlds were secure, that Diti was tormented by sorrow.
Burning with grief for her sons, crying out 'Alas, alas!', senseless, / to her husband, who was like the sun, endowed with the fiery energy of asceticism,
the giver, the great-souled husband Kaśyapa at that time, / bowing with devotion, O best of brahmins, she spoke to him of great mind:
'O Venerable One, my sons have been destroyed, done by the disc-wielding God; / all the daiteyas and dānavas have been struck down by the gods.
I am burning with the fire of grief for my sons, O best among sages. / Give me a son who will bring me delight, taking away all their fiery energy, O Lord,
very strong, with handsome limbs, having splendor equal to the king of the gods, / intelligent, omniscient, knowledgeable, learned in everything,
endowed with the fiery energy of asceticism, powerful, possessing handsome marks, / devoted to sacred learning, knower of wisdom, worshipper of gods and brahmins,
conqueror of all worlds, bringing me delight, O twice-born one, / endowed with all auspicious marks; give me a son, O Lord.'
Having heard these excellent words of hers, Kaśyapa, / his mind filled with compassion, was pleased, O best of the twice-born, with the sorrowful woman.
That fortunate one spoke to the wretched woman whose mind was miserable; / placing his hand upon her head, devoted to deep affection [he said]:
'O fortunate one, a son such as you desire will come to be.' / Having spoken thus, he went to Meru, the best of supreme mountains.
Without any support, fulfilling a supreme vow, he performed asceticism. / In the meantime, she bore an excellent embryo.
That Diti, knowing all dharma, of beautiful deeds, wise-minded, / for the duration of a hundred years remained pure-hearted.
By her was born indeed a son endowed with the fiery energy of Brahmā. / Then Kaśyapa arrived, filled with great joy.
The wise one, best of men, gave a name to that son; / he called his son Bala, [saying], 'He is great, worthy of the name.'
Having thus named him, he then performed the sacred-thread investiture; / he spoke to his son: 'O fortunate one, accomplish Vedic studentship.'
'Indeed, just so I shall do your bidding, O best of the twice-born; / I shall pursue the study of the Veda through Vedic studentship, O best of beings.'
Thus a full hundred years passed for him as he performed austerities. / He came before his mother, endowed with the fiery energy of asceticism.
The divine studentship of that great-souled one, full of the heroism of asceticism, / Diti beheld in her son, filled with great joy.
She spoke to the great-souled Bala, her ascetic son, / who was intelligent, great-souled, skilled in discernment and wisdom:
'While you live, O intelligent one, my sons live again— / those such as Hiraṇyakaśipu who were slain by the disc-wielder.
Avenge this enmity for me, child; slay the gods, your enemies, in battle.' / Then Danu spoke this to Bala, her very strong son:
'At first, O son, quickly destroy Indra, the king of the gods; / afterwards, let the gods be struck down, and then the one who rides Garuḍa.'
Having overheard the two of them, that goddess Aditi, who regarded her husband as her deity, / filled with great sorrow, spoke to her son Indra:
'The son of Diti, of vast body, is growing through the fiery energy of Brahmā; / for the slaughter of the gods he has performed asceticism, stainless one.
Know this, O Lord of the gods, if you desire welfare here.' / Having heard those words of his mother, the subjugator of Pāka,
the king of the gods, then fell into great anxiety through sorrow; / terrified by great fear, he then pondered:
'How shall I kill him, the defiler of divine dharma?' / Having thus resolved, the Lord of the gods, on the destruction of Bala,
once indeed, when that Bala had resorted to the sea for the twilight devotion, / shining with a divine black antelope skin and a wooden staff,
along with that pure, holy studentship of his, / near the ocean, having come to the twilight prayer seat,
muttering prayers, very peaceful, the subjugator of Pāka saw him; / with that divine thunderbolt, the son of Diti was struck.
Seeing Bala fallen on the ground, his life-breath gone, / the king of the gods, filled with great joy, then rejoiced.
Having thus struck down that daitya, the delight of Diti, / the righteous subjugator of Pāka ruled in happiness.

2.24.m: Sūta said: / Having heard that her son Bala, and Subala, was slain, / weeping pitifully [she cried]: 'Alas, alas, great is my misery!'
Having thus wept most pitifully for a long time, the ascetic woman, / that renowned woman, went to her beloved Kaśyapa and spoke to him:
'Your son Indra, the ruler of the divine hosts, very wicked, / seeing my Bala, who possessed the marks of Brahmā, approached to the ocean,
slew him with his thunderbolt, even as he was engaged in the twilight devotion.' / Having heard this, the son of Marīci was then enraged.
Filled with great anger, he blazed as if with fire; / plucking out a matted lock, that best of the twice-born cast it into the pure fire:
'I produce a son solely for the destruction of Indra.' / From that sacrificial pit, even from the mouth of the fire, there arose [a being]
endowed with the hue of a heap of black collyrium, reddish-brown-eyed, of terrifying appearance, / with mouth and fangs gaping frightfully, striking terror into the worlds,
terrible, of mighty frame, holding sword and shield, / blazing in all limbs with fiery energy, mighty, like a great raincloud.
He said to the brahmin Kaśyapa: 'Let a command be given to me. / For what reason have I been produced by you, O brahmin? Tell me the cause.
I will accomplish it by your grace, O one of noble vows.' / Kaśyapa said: 'Fulfill the desire of this woman, and of myself, my son;
slay wicked Indra, of Aditi, O greatly wise one; / when the king of the gods is slain, enjoy the station of Indra, indeed.'
Having thus been instructed by that great-souled Kaśyapa, / Vṛtra made an effort for the slaying of that Indra.
And he practiced the science of archery, filled with prowess; / [he showed] strength, heroism, kṣatriya martial power, endowed with fiery energy and fortitude.
Seeing him, the thousand-eyed Indra was distressed with fear of that daitya; / he considered a means against that wicked-minded Vṛtra.
For the purpose of his slaying, the god of gods, having summoned the great sages, / dispatched the seven sages to Vṛtra, the ruler of the daityas.
"Let your honors go there where Vṛtra is staying. / Make an alliance with him on my behalf, O lords of sages!"
Thus commanded by him, those seven sages then, / dispatched by the Thousand-Eyed One, said to the asura Vṛtra:
"He extends friendship; let it be accepted, O best of daityas!" / The seven sages, knowers of reality, said to the mighty Vṛtra:
"The very wise Thousand-Eyed One wishes to make friendship / with you, O best one! Why then do you not do so?
Enjoy happily, O hero, half of the realm of Indra! / Let Indra live with half, and let the asuras and gods,
all of them, dwell in happiness, abandoning their enmity." / Vṛtra said: "If the lord of gods, the most virtuous one, truly desires friendship,
then, relying on truth, I will do so, there is no doubt of this. / [Yet,] putting deceit first, should Indra practice treachery,
what is to be done then, O brāhmaṇas? What guarantee is there in this matter?" / The sages, however, said to Indra: "State a pledge for this matter;
tell us the truth of this, if you desire friendship here." / Indra said: "If I act falsely with you, using deceit,
may I be stained by sins like the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt of this! / If, putting deceit first, Indra should practice treachery,
may I be stained by sins like the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt of this! / Thus that Puraṃdara of great wisdom said to you.
Even with this guarantee, make friendship, O broad-minded one!" / Vṛtra said: "Following the path of the cultured shown by your honors, and through this truth of his,
I will make friendship with him, O best among the twice-born!" / Vṛtra was led to Indra's dwelling by the eminent brāhmaṇas.
Seeing Vṛtra arrive, Indra, ready for friendship, / rose from his throne and, quickly taking an offering of water,
the righteous one gave it to Vṛtra, O best of the twice-born: / "Enjoy, O very wise one, half of this great realm of Indra!
We two must live in happiness, O best of daityas!" / Thus, winning the trust of the daitya Vṛtra with friendship at that time,
when those brāhmaṇas had gone to their own abode, O best of the twice-born, / the wicked-minded one was always looking for a weakness in Vṛtra.
Indra thought day and night with alertness; / yet he could see no weakness in the great-souled Vṛtra.
He devised a scheme for the sake of killing him: / Rambhā was sent by him: "Bewilder the great asura!
Act in such a way, O fortunate lady, for the infatuation of the enemy of the gods, / so that, having slain him by some means, I may attain peace!"
There was a holy, most divine forest, frequented by sacred trees, / endowed with many fruit-bearing trees, crowded with beasts and birds,
adorned everywhere with heavenly celestial-chariot temples, / with divine gandharva songs, constantly teeming with bees,
everywhere sweet and resonant with the sacred cries of cuckoos, / and densely filled everywhere with the cries of peacocks and deer,
adorned on all sides with divine sandalwood trees, / and with charming ponds, pools, and lakes filled with water,
adorned with blossomed lotuses and hundred-petaled water-lilies; / with gods, gandharvas, perfected beings, cāraṇas, and kinnaras,
and with divine sages, it shone, being an excellent heavenly garden, / crowded with hosts of apsarases, with various wondrous and auspicious sights,
crowded with golden palaces, adorned everywhere / with staves, parasols, chowries, jars, and banners,
filled with the sound of the Vedas, resonant with the sound of song. / Having reached Nandana thus, that Rambhā of charming smile,
a wanton woman, sported there together with the apsarases. / Sūta said: / Once, drawn by time, that Vṛtra went to the forest,
accompanied by several dānavas, filled with supreme joy. / Unnoticed, [Indra] roamed near that great-souled one.
The king of the gods too, O best of brāhmaṇas, was indeed searching for a weakness in his enemy. / But that Vṛtra of great wisdom was trusting in all his deeds;
knowing Indra to be his highest friend, he had no fear of him. / Wandering about, he beheld the forest, supremely auspicious everywhere,
a delightful pleasure-grove crowded with multitudes of women. / Taking refuge in the cool, deeply auspicious shade
of a sandalwood tree, large-eyed Rambhā was playing there, / mounted on a swing with her female companions, the illustrious, celebrated one.
She sang a sweet-voiced song that enchanted the whole world. / There Vṛtra arrived, his mind agitated by desire,
having seen Rambhā of lovely and beautiful eyes mounted on the swing.

2.25.m: Sūta said: / "Who indeed is this sweet-eyed one singing, who enchants the entire world with her graceful charms? / The young maiden shone exceedingly charming; with her complete amorous expressions she would bewilder any person!"

Seeing Rambhā, who had eyes broad as lotus petals, swelling breasts, and limbs smeared with saffron: / "With her lotus-like face, she is the abode of love for me! Or is this charming, lovely maiden Rati herself?

Endowed with full charms and supreme beauty, possessing a nature inclined to love's ways and utmost gentleness, / I will fall under her control right here; today I have been sent right here by the mind-born god of love!"
Thus the daitya, engrossed in deep contemplation, captivated by love and impelled by prolonged longing, / greatly afflicted, went there swiftly and, his mind humbled, said to the fair-eyed lady:

"Whose are you, O beautiful woman, and by whom have you been sent? What is your most auspicious name? Tell me! / By your very form of immense radiance, I am infatuated, O young girl; come under my control!"
Thus addressed, the large-eyed woman [said] to Vṛtra who was agitated by passion: / "I am Rambhā, O noble one, [come] for sport to the excellent forest.
Together with my female companions I have come to the excellent Nandana grove. / But who are you, and for what purpose have you approached me?"
Vṛtra said: / "Listen, I will tell who I am that have come, O maiden: / born from the fire, I am the son of Kaśyapa, O fair one!
I am the friend of the god of gods, of Indra, O woman of lovely face! / Half of the realm of Indra, O woman of beautiful hips, has come into my enjoyment.
I am Vṛtra; how is it, O lady, that you do not know me as such, / under whose control the three worlds have fallen, O woman of excellent complexion?
I have come for refuge; protect me from desire, O fair-faced one! / Accept me, O large-eyed one, agitated by passion, O beloved!"
Rambhā said: / "I shall today come under your control, there is no doubt; / whatever I say, O hero, that very thing must be done by you!"
[Vṛtra said:] "Let it be so, O illustrious lady! I will do each and every thing!" / Having thus made an agreement with her, the mighty one,
the best of dānavas, took delight in that most sacred forest / through her song, dance, laughter, and graceful charm.
The great daitya was utterly captivated by her sexual intimacy. / She said to that illustrious Vṛtra, the best of dānavas:
"Drink wine here; drink sweet mādhavī liquor!" / [And] he spoke to that large-eyed Rambhā, whose face was like the moon:
"I am the son of a brāhmaṇa, master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas. / How can I drink liquor, O blessed lady, which is condemned?"
Then liquor was given by force by that goddess Rambhā out of passion; / out of courtesy toward her, he then drank the liquor.
When, completely intoxicated with liquor, he lost his good judgment, / right at that moment he was struck down with the vajra by the lord of the gods.
Stained then by the sins of killing a brāhmaṇa and the like, Vṛtra's slayer / was addressed by the brāhmaṇas: "Indra, you have committed a sin!
Having placed his trust in our word, the mighty Vṛtra by name / was killed through [his] feeling of trust; thus a sin has been committed by you."
Indra said: / "By whatever means, an enemy must always be slain. / The slayer of gods and brāhmaṇas, the thorn in the side of sacrifices and dharma—
that wicked demon who had become the ruler of the three worlds has been killed. / You are angry on his account; is this the mark of justice?
Deliberation should be conducted thus by you, best among the twice-born; / afterwards anger may be displayed; let my injustice be considered!"
Having been thus instructed by the great-souled Indra / and instructed by all the gods headed by Brahmā, those excellent men
went indeed to their own abode when that thorn to dharma had been slain.

2.26.m: Sūta said: / Hearing that her son had been killed, that Diti was afflicted with grief; / she was utterly consumed by that grief for her son, O best of the twice-born.
Again she spoke to the great-souled Kaśyapa, the foremost among sages, / for the destruction of the very wicked Indra, O best of the twice-born:
"One son, full of fierce brāhmaṇical splendor, unbearable to all the deities, / should be granted to me, beloved husband, since I am your dearest, O lord!"
Kaśyapa said: / "Bala and Vṛtra, both mighty sons of mine, were slain / by the god Indra, that evil-souled one, resorting to sin.
For his very destruction I shall grant [you] a single son. / But remain pure for a full hundred years, O illustrious lady."
Having spoken thus, that lord of yogins, placing his hand upon [her] head, / went together with Diti straight to the Meru penance-grove.
Dwelling in the penance-grove, that goddess performed austerity, / remaining always pure for the sake of a son, O best of the twice-born.
Then the thousand-eyed god [Indra], having learned of her endeavor, / looked for a vulnerability in Diti, O blessed one.
Having assumed the form of a twenty-five-year-old, divine in appearance, / in the form of a brāhmaṇa, the king of the gods came into her presence.
Bowing to that virtuous mother endowed with austerity, / the thousand-eyed one was asked by her: "Who are you, O best of the twice-born?"
The thousand-eyed one said to her: "I am your son, O fair lady; / I am a brāhmaṇa, learned in the Veda, and I know dharma, O radiant lady.
I shall assist you in your austerities; of this there is no doubt." / He served that virtuous goddess, his mother, endowed with austerity.
She did not know that Indra, the committer of evil, had arrived; / she thought of him as a son of dharma as he served her day by day.
He would massage the limbs of the goddess, wash her feet, / and provide leaf, root, fruit, bark garments, and deerskin.
Thus that righteous one continually gave to that Diti; / pleased by his devotion and contented, she said to him:
"When the most meritorious son is born and Indra is slain, / rule over the heavenly kingdom, O blessed one, together with my son!"
"So be it, O blessed lady; by your grace it will come to pass." / But the tamer of Pāka was constantly watching for a lapse of hers.
When her hundred years were nearly complete, the infallible one saw a lapse: / without washing her feet, Diti got into bed.
Having placed her head at the [foot of the] bed, with hair unloosed and deeply overcome, / she fell into sleep. Having entered her belly,
the vajra-handed one then cut the fetus into seven parts / with his sharp-edged vajra. Remaining in the belly, he wept.
As that fetus fell into the hands of Indra, O leaders among brāhmaṇas, / he spoke again and again to that mighty fetus as it wept.
Śatakratu of great splendor said: "Do not cry!" / Śakra again cut that fetus born of Diti into seven parts;
having cut each one into seven parts as it wept, that king of the gods— / thus indeed the Maruts were born, those gods of great majesty.
According to the way Indra addressed them, their names came to be; / possessing extraordinary strength and huge bodies, with fierce brilliance and valor,
they became forty-nine Maruts in total. / Known by the name Maruts, they took refuge in Indra alone.
They are pleasing to the great host of all beings. / Hari, the lord of creatures, assigned among the various classes
those kingdoms in due order, beginning with that of Pṛthu. / That god is the puruṣa Kṛṣṇa, all-pervading, the teacher of the world,
conquering through austerity, of great splendor, the one Prajāpati of all, / Parjanya, the holy Fire, the self of all, and indeed everything.
All this holy universe, moving and unmoving, belongs to him. / To one who knows properly this creation of beings, O best of the twice-born,
there is no fear of return here; whence could there be fear of the other world? / This most holy, auspicious creation that removes all sins—
the person who listens to it with devotion is freed from all sins; / he is indeed fortunate, meritorious, and endowed with truth.
Whoever listens to [the account of] this creation goes to the supreme state; / his self fully purified of all sin, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

2.27.m: Sūta said: / That lord, the ruler of all the worlds, then consecrated King / Pṛthu, the son of Vena, the great sovereign over all the realm,
large-armed and large-bodied, just like Indra, lord of the gods. / Then, having deliberated upon the kingdoms in succession, Brahmā
began to bestow whatever was fitting for each one. / Over trees, brāhmaṇas, planets, and constellations,
the great-minded one consecrated Soma in kingship, and over penances, / dharmas, righteous sacrifices, holy ones, and those of holy splendor;
likewise the god Varuṇa in the midst of waters and sacred bathing places, / having consecrated him, and over jewels, O best among the twice-born;
moreover, Vaiśravaṇa in kingship over all the other yakṣas; / and the grandfather [Brahmā] established the greatly wise Viṣṇu
in kingship over the Ādityas for the sake of the welfare of the people; / and Dakṣa the prajāpati over all the holy ones;
capable, knower of all dharma, and lord of the host of Prajāpatis; / he established Prahrāda, the knower of all dharma,
endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu, over the daityas and dānavas; / and having consecrated Yama, the son of Vivasvat, Dharma, in the realm of the ancestors;
over the yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, serpents, crawling beings, / and over all the yoginīs and great vaitālas,
and over all the kaṅkālas and kūṣmāṇḍas likewise, / and over all earthly lords, Giriśa, the trident-handed [Śiva];
and over all mountains, the great mountain Himavat; / and over rivers, reservoirs, and step-wells,

And in the divine realm of ponds, reservoirs, and wells, the lord of gods
established the sacred ocean, the supreme [place of pilgrimage] of all sacred places.

And likewise, in the sacred realm of all the Gandharvas,
the lord of gods, Brahmā, then consecrated Citraratha.

And over the Nāgas of sacred valor, the Four-faced One [consecrated] Vāsuki;
and in the realm of snakes, he consecrated Takṣaka.

Then, over the realm of elephants, he consecrated Airāvata;
and over all horses, Uccaiḥśravas.

And over all birds, he [consecrated] Garuḍa;
and over the realm of beasts, Brahmā then designated the lion.

Having consecrated the bull among cattle, the Prajāpati,
the Grandfather, [consecrated] the plakṣa tree over all trees.

Having thus established all the kingdoms, the Grandfather,
Brahmā, the best of beings, then appointed guardians of the directions.

In the eastern quarter, the best of beings consecrated as king
Sudhanvan, the son of Vairāja, as guardian of the direction.

In the south, he consecrated as king the high-souled Śaṅkhapada,
the son of the Prajāpati Kardama.

Likewise, in the west, the Prajāpati Brahmā consecrated
Puṣkara, the son of the Prajāpati Varuṇa.

And in the northern quarter, O brāhmaṇa, [he consecrated] Nalakūbara;
and in this way, he consecrated the guardians of the directions of great splendor,

by whom this entire earth, with its seven continents and its cities,
is protected according to law in each region even today.

And thus the illustrious Pṛthu was consecrated as ruler of men,
consecrated with all great sacrifices beginning with the Rājasūya,

according to the rule seen in the Vedas, as lord of the earth in royal sovereignty.
And when the glorious, sacred [manvantara] named Cākṣuṣa had passed,

O illustrious one, in that manvantara which desired the good of the gods and merit,
he then assigned the kingdom to Manu Vaivasvata.

And I will explain in detail concerning the high-souled Pṛthu,
if, O best of vipras, you wish to listen to me with diligence.

This seat [of narration] is celebrated as greatly meritorious;
indeed, in all the Purāṇas this is forever established.

It is sacred, conferring renown, longevity, auspicious, giving residence in heaven,
auspicious, pure, life-prolonging, giving sons, and granting prosperity.

The man who hears it with devotion, endowed with devotional feeling and meditation,
receives the fruit of a horse sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.

2.28.m:
The ṛṣis said:
Explain in detail the birth of that high-souled one,
of Pṛthu, O illustrious one! We wish to hear [it] again:

how by that king, that high-souled one, this earth was milked,
and then by gods, ancestors, and sages who know the truth;

how by Daityas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, trees,
mountains, Piśācas, and Gandharvas of sacred deeds;

how previously it was milked by brāhmaṇas, Siddhas, and Rākṣasas of terrible prowess,
and by other very great souls.

State to us, O great-minded one, their specific holding of the vessel
and the rule regarding the milk, as well as the special [yield] for all of them.

And why, previously, in this world, was the arm of the high-souled king Vena
churned by the ṛṣis?

Tell us, O Sūta's son, why he was angered by those of great merit.
This story is wondrous, sacred, and destroys all sins.

We desire to hear it, O illustrious one; satisfaction is never reached.
Sūta said:
Concerning Pṛthu, the son of Vena, and his detail,

his birth, valor, field, and manliness, O best of twice-born ones,
I will proclaim all the conduct of that wise one.

Listen to me in this way, O illustrious ones, O best of twice-born ones:
it should not be told to an unfaithful person, to one lacking faith, to a rogue,

to a total fool, to one deeply deluded, nor likewise to a bad disciple,
nor to one devoid of faith, nor to a deceitful one; do not, O twice-born ones, [tell it] for total destruction!

Whoever recites it otherwise indeed goes to hell.
You are endowed with devotion, dedicated to truth and dharma.

Before you I will completely proclaim the entire conduct
which destroys sins; listen, O best of twice-born ones!

Conferring heaven, renown, and longevity, auspicious, equal to the Vedas,
a secret revealed by the ṛṣis, I will proclaim, O best of twice-born ones.

And whoever constantly recites this detail of Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
having bowed to the brāhmaṇas, does not grieve over what was done or left undone.

Sin accumulated in seven births is destroyed merely by hearing it.
A brāhmaṇa becomes learned in the Vedas, and a kṣatriya becomes victorious;

a vaiśya becomes rich in wealth, and a śūdra attains happiness.
Such fruit does one obtain from reading and also from hearing [it].

The birth and deeds of Pṛthu are pure and sin-destroying;
he was a guardian of dharma, very wise, skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and śāstras.

Born in the lineage of Atri, previously equal to Atri, a lord,
a creator of all dharma, was a Prajāpati named Aṅga.

The son who was his was a Prajāpati named Vena;
he, abandoning dharma, always acted [otherwise].

The daughter of Mṛtyu was the illustrious Sunīthā by name;
that illustrious Aṅga married her, Sunīthā.

Upon her he fathered Vena, the destroyer of dharma.
Through the fault of his maternal grandfather, Vena, the grandson of the god of death,

abandoning his own dharma, became devoted to adharma;
out of desire, greed, and great delusion, he committed only sin.

Abandoning the dharma consisting of Vedic conduct, the ruler of men
followed sinful ways, deluded by pride and envy.

People in the world then proceeded without Vedic study;
under that Prajāpati, the subjects were without Vedic recitation and without the cry of vaṣaṭ.

The deities did not drink the offered soma poured in sacrifices.
Thus that evil-minded one spoke constantly to the brāhmaṇas:

"No study is to be done, no oblation offered, no gift given,
no sacrifice performed, and no offering made"—such was that Prajāpati's

cruel decree, when destruction was imminent.
"I am the object of sacrifice, I am the sacrificer, and I am the sacrifice," he said repeatedly.

"Sacrifices are to be performed unto me, oblations are to be poured unto me"—
thus Vena constantly said: "Indeed, I am the eternal Viṣṇu.

I am Brahmā, I am Rudra, Mitra, Indra, and the wind;
I alone am the enjoyer of the offerings to gods and ancestors, no doubt."

Then those sages of great power, angered at Vena,
all assembled and spoke to that king of sinful mind.

The ṛṣis said:
A king is the lord of the earth; he constantly protects the subjects.
He is the embodiment of dharma, O king of kings; therefore, he should indeed protect dharma.

We are about to enter initiation for a twelve-year sacrifice;
do not cause adharma in the sacrifice; this dharma is the path of the good.

Practice dharma, O great king; act truthfully and righteously!
'I shall protect the subjects'—such is the pledge made by you."

To all those great ṛṣis speaking thus, then,
the evil-minded Vena laughed and spoke this senseless matter:
Vena said: / 'Who else is the creator of dharma, or whom should I listen to? / Who on earth is my equal in sacred learning, valor, ascetic power, and truth?
The origin of all beings, and of all dharmas in particular— / surely you confused, senseless men do not know me!'
'If I wish, I could burn the earth, or flood it with waters, / and block both heaven and earth; on this point no doubt should be entertained!'
When, O king, Vena could not be turned away / from his delusion and arrogance, the great seers became enraged.
Seizing the trembling Vena by force with anger, / their wrath aroused, they churned his left thigh.
Endowed with the hue of a heap of black collyrium, very short, misshapen, / long-faced, ugly-eyed, with the luster of a blue tunic,
pot-bellied, broad-eared, terrified, and repulsive— / those noble seers saw him and said to him: 'Sit down (niṣīda)!'
Hearing their command, stricken with terror, he sat down. / In the mountains and forests his lineage became established:
The Niṣādas, Kirātas, Bhillas, Nahalakas, / Bhramaras, Pulindas, and whatever other Mleccha tribes there are,
practicing evil ways—all of them were born from that limb. / Then all those seers, with calmed minds,
seeing that the best of kings, Vena, had thus become free from impurity, / churned the right hand of that noble one.
As his hand was churned, sweat alone was produced; / again those brahmins churned his right hand.
From that auspicious hand arose a man resembling the twelve suns, / his limbs having the color of molten gold, covered in divine garlands and garments,
his limbs adorned with divine ornaments, anointed with divine fragrant pastes, / shining with a sun-colored crown and two earrings,
huge-bodied, long-armed, peerless in form on the earth, / holding a sword and arrows, armed with a bow, clad in armor, a great lord,
endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with all ornaments, / exceedingly wise, [resplendent] with splendor, beauty, and golden luster.
Just as Indra shines in heaven, so the son of Vena shone on earth. / When that noble one was born, the gods and pure seers
all celebrated a festival on account of Vena’s son, / who shone with his own body like fire personified, blazing,
holding the primeval, supreme bow named Ājagava, / divine arrows for protection, and armor of great brilliance.
When that noble, heroic, and great-souled Pṛthu was born, / all creatures rejoiced greatly, O best of the twice-born.
All the sacred waters and various holy streams, / O chiefs of brahmins, set out for his consecration.
The gods headed by the Grandfather [Brahmā], and various beings, / both stationary and moving, consecrated the ruler of men,
the great hero, the protector of subjects, Pṛthu himself, O best of the twice-born. / Approaching Pṛthu, the son of Vena, to the kingship over kings, the moving and unmoving beings,
along with all the gods and brahmins, consecrated that noble-minded one; / Pṛthu, the powerful son of Vena, was indeed consecrated to supreme sovereignty over kings.
All the subjects had never been pleased by his father; / pleased by him, they all rejoiced in happiness.
From the affection (anurāga) [he inspired], that hero received the name 'king' (rājan). / When that brave hero approached the ocean, O best of the twice-born,
all the waters stood still out of fear of that noble one. / Clearing difficult routes, the mountains gave him easy paths.
Those mountains did not break his banners. / The earth bore crops without being plowed; everywhere cows yielded all desires.
The rain cloud rained according to wish; all the brahmins / and the Kṣatriyas and others performed great festivals with Vedic sacrifices.
The trees bore fruit fulfilling every wish while that king was ruling; / there was no famine, no disease, and no premature death among men.
All people lived in happiness, dedicated to dharma, / while that invincible king of kings, the noble one, ruled.
At that very time, during the auspicious sacrifice of the Grandfather [Brahmā], / the Sūta was born from the extraction of Soma on an auspicious day of that noble one.
At that very great sacrifice, the wise Māgadha was also born. / For the praise of Pṛthu, the two were summoned there by the great seers.
I shall describe the character of a Sūta, which is very auspicious, O best of the twice-born: / equipped with topknot and sacred thread, devoted to Vedic recitation,
knowing the meaning of all treatises, he attends to the Agnihotra, / endowed with generosity and study, dedicated to the conduct of a brahmin,
always delighting in worshiping the gods and brahmins; / as a bard, he may sacrifice with your holy Vedic mantras.
Always devoted to the conduct of a brahmin, having kinship with brahmins— / thus he was born. The Māgadha is devoid of Vedic recitation.
All the Bandins and Cāraṇas are devoid of the conduct of a brahmin; / they are to be known, O blessed ones, as praise-singers of rulers.
Both the skilled Sūta and Māgadha were created for singing praise. / All the seers said to them: 'Let this king be praised
with deeds appropriate to him, corresponding to what this ruler of men is like.' / Then both the Bandin and the Māgadha said to all those seers:
'We two please gods and seers with our own deeds; / yet we do not know his deeds, nor his qualities, nor his fame.
By what deed should we compose praise for this noble one? / O chiefs of brahmins, we do not know them, for his virtues are unknown.'
'This best of men should be praised with those holy virtues that will come to be, / and with the deeds that Pṛthu of great renown will perform.'
All those sages declared the divine qualities of the noble one: / 'He will be truthful, endowed with knowledge, wise, of celebrated valor,
ever heroic, appreciating virtues, righteous, renouncing, virtuous, / pious, speaking the truth, and the best of sacrificers in sacrifices,
pleasant-spoken, truthful, wealthy in grain, wealthy in riches, virtuous, / discerning of qualities, receptive to virtues, knower of dharma, affectionate to truth,
