all-pervading, all-knowing, devoted to brahmins, knowing the Veda, wise, / prudent, endowed with a melodious voice, proficient in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas,
the creator and protector of subjects, victorious on the battlefield, / the best of kings, who in sacrifices such as the Rājasūya
will be the sole performer on earth, endowed with all virtues. / These qualities will indeed exist in the person of this noble one.'
Directed by the seers, the Sūta and Māgadha then / composed the praise of that noble one with those future virtues.
From that time forward, O wise one, kings are pleased with praises; / and in their presence, people will become donors through eulogies of virtue.
From that time forward in this world, O best of the twice-born, / blessings are employed in praises, and supreme wealth is given to them.
To the Sūta, to the Māgadha, and to the Bandin he gave great prosperity; / then he gave the excellent Tailaṅga country to the Cāraṇa.
Out of graciousness, the righteous Pṛthu, the prince, gave the Haihaya country as well, / having founded a city after his own name on the bank of the Revā.
In ancient times Pṛthu, sacrificing, gave [wealth] to the brahmins, O best of the twice-born— / [honoring him,] the omniscient, the giver of everything, powerful in righteousness, the best of men.
All the subjects and the sages, whose impurities were removed by asceticism, looked upon him; / the virtuous ones said to one another: "This king is highly intelligent.
He is the granter of livelihood to the gods and others, and especially to us; / he is the protector of the subjects, and he indeed will grant us livelihood.
This nurse [of creatures], highly wise, swallowed the seeds sown of old / by the subjects for their survival, and then became motionless."
Then, O best of the twice-born, the subjects rushed to Pṛthu: / "Provide us with a good livelihood!" Such was the word of the sages then.
Having swallowed the foodgrains then, the earth became utterly motionless; / seeing the very great distress of the subjects, the best of kings,
upon the word of the great sages, took up his bow together with an arrow; / angry, the king rushed with speed toward the earth.
Assuming the form of an elephant out of fear of him, the earth / roamed about hidden in forests and impassable regions.
The highly intelligent one did not see her in an altered form, O best of the twice-born; / [the sages] told the highly intelligent one: "She has assumed the form of an elephant."
Then the king rushed upon her in the form of an elephant; / and she was then struck by him with sharp arrows.
Assuming the form of a lion, she became intent on fleeing; / [but] assuming the form of Hari, the king rushed upon her.
Extremely enraged, the highly intelligent one, his fine eyes red with fury, / struck the earth with sharp, keen arrows.
She became agitated and bewildered, struck by the impact of the arrows; / assuming the form of a female buffalo, she became intent on fleeing.
Holding a bow, arrow in hand, he rushed with speed; / becoming a cow, O best of the twice-born, she went straight to heaven.
She went for refuge to Brahmā and to the great-souled Viṣṇu, / and to gods such as Rudra, but found no place of rescue.
Finding no refuge at all, she returned only to the son of Vena; / distressed by the blows of his arrows, she returned to his side.
Folding her hands in reverence, she spoke these words to Pṛthu; / "Save me, save me, O king of kings!" she said to the king.
"I am the nurse, O fortunate one, the earth who supports all; / if I am killed, O king, the seven worlds are destroyed.
Folding her hands in reverence, she who is ever to be revered by the three worlds / spoke to this king: "A woman is never to be killed, O king.
A great sin is perceived by the best of the twice-born in the slaying of women; / a great sin is perceived by the best of the twice-born in the slaying of cows.
Without me, O great king, how will you support the subjects? / When I am steady, O king, then the moving and unmoving worlds
attain steadiness, for they are established when I am made steady; / but without me these worlds, both moving and unmoving, would perish.
Then the subjects would perish if my destruction were to come; / and how will you support the subjects without me, O king?
In me the worlds are steady, O king; by me this universe is supported; / if I am destroyed, all the subjects would perish without a doubt.
You ought not to kill me if you desire the welfare / of the subjects, O protector of the earth; listen to my word, O divine ruler!
Undertakings attain complete success through means, O fortunate one; / therefore, consider a means by which you will support the subjects.
If you kill me, O great king, in supporting, protecting always, / and nourishing, O highly intelligent one, how indeed without me, O king,
will you support the subjects? Curb your anger! / I will become full of food, and I will support these subjects.
I am a woman and not to be killed, and you would have to perform penance; / for they say a female is not to be killed, even if she belongs to the animal realm.
Reflecting thus, O great king, you ought to renounce unrighteousness." / Addressed thus with words of various kinds by the nurse [of all], the king [was beseeched]:
"O great king, renounce this dreadful anger! / When you are pleased, O king of kings, then I shall become well."
Addressed thus by her, the king, Pṛthu the son of Vena, lord of creatures, / spoke to that highly fortunate earth, O best of the twice-born.

2.29.m: Pṛthu said: / "When a single great sinner of wicked conduct is killed, / creatures live happily, and the virtuous behold merit.
Therefore, one evil, evil-minded individual should be struck down; / therefore, I shall indeed slay you, the destroyer of all living beings.
By you all these seeds have been hidden at present; / having swallowed them and become motionless, after slaying the subjects, where will you go?
When a wicked evildoer is slain, the virtuous live happily; / therefore, evil must be struck down; this is the truth, without a doubt.
That from which righteousness increases must be protected with effort; / but by you a great sin has been committed, causing the ruin of the subjects.
If one kills a tormentor of the world for the sake of a single person, / whether for oneself or for another, he incurs no sin.
If many will attain happiness when one auspicious [being] is slain, / O earth, when an evil one is slain, there is neither major sin nor minor sin.
For the sake of the subjects I will certainly kill you, without a doubt, / if you do not carry out my word which is conjoined with virtue.
For the sake of the welfare of this world, and properly, O earth, / I will slay you with sharp arrows if you turn away from my command.
By my own splendor I shall indeed support the virtuous subjects / dwelling in the three worlds, and in accordance with righteousness, without a doubt.
Abiding by my command, which is united with righteousness, O earth, / enliven these subjects perpetually by my order.
If you act according to my command, O blessed one, / then I will be pleased with you and will protect you always.
Indeed you [will be protected], without a doubt, and other best of kings [will do so too]." / In the form of a cow, the earth, her body pierced with arrows,
spoke thus to Pṛthu, the son of Vena, the foundation of righteousness, the highly intelligent one. / The earth said: / "Your command, O great king, which is endowed with truth, merit, and purpose,
I will execute completely for the sake of the subjects, without a doubt. / Even through righteous effort and appropriate means, O lord of men,
undertakings and virtuous enterprises succeed; / see the means, O king of kings, by which you may remain true to your word,
and by which you may support these subjects so that I may foster all of them. / And these excellent arrows, whetted on stone, are lodged in my limbs;
pull them out yourself, O king; they torment me severely! / Make me level, O great king, so that milk may remain in me."
Sūta said: / With the tip of his bow, pushing away those various and heavy mountains, / he then made the whole [earth] level.
From that time forth, those mountains grew in size, O best of the twice-born; / having himself extracted his own arrows from her limbs,
the son of Vena then, with a pleased mind, / leveled the pits and caverns with the impact of his arrows.
Thus the promoter of virtue made the whole earth level; / having leveled it, the highly fortunate one arranged a calf for her,
having contemplated again and again the former Svāyambhuva Manu, / when all the Manvantaras had passed, O best of men.
The earth had become uneven, and there was no path anywhere; / thus, O best of the twice-born, the level and the uneven [tracts] had arisen on their own.
Formerly, when the interval of the Manu Cākṣuṣa had arrived, / and the previous creation had taken place on the uneven surface of the earth,
no boundary was seen / of villages, cities, towns, regions, or arable fields.
Neither agriculture, nor trade, nor cattle-rearing went on; / no one spoke untruth, nor was there greed or malice.
Indeed, no one ever showed arrogance or committed sin. / When the interval of Vaivasvata arrived, O best of the twice-born,
prior to the birth of the son of Vena, the creatures came into being; / all these creatures, O twice-born, chose their dwelling-places:
here on the ground, somewhere on a mountain, or along riverbanks, / in bowers, at all holy bathing-places, and on the shores of the ocean.
All creatures made their dwelling there through merit alone; / their food consisted of fruits, roots, and honey.
Their sustenance was obtained with great difficulty, O best of the twice-born. / Seeing the distress of the creatures, Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
made the Manu Svāyambhuva the calf, that king; / and his own hand was made the vessel, O wise one.
Then that Pṛthu, a tiger among men, milked the earth / of milk consisting of all crops, endowed with all foods and virtues.
With that meritorious food, comparable to nectar, those creatures / bring satisfaction to the gods, and the creatures [do so] likewise to the ancestors and others.
By the grace of that son of Vena, those creatures live in comfort; / having offered food to the gods and to the ancestors, the creatures then,
Especially to the brāhmaṇas and likewise to the guests, / afterwards all those meritorious subjects eat, O best of the twice-born.
And through sacrifices others sacrifice, gratifying Janārdana; / with that food, the deities and the lord of the gods attain satisfaction.
The rain-cloud, sent by Mādhava, rains again; / from that, the sacred, mighty medicinal plants arise, conferring great merit.
All varieties of grain [were produced by] Pṛthu, the son of Vena, the lord of creatures; / on that food, all creatures subsist continually even today.
And thus this earth was milked by the sages gathered together, / and again by the highly fortunate, truthful Brahmins and gods.
Soma became the calf, and the preceptor of the gods himself was the milker; / [the milk was] vigor, the milk resembling nectar, by which the immortals live.
By their truth and merit, all living beings subsist; / they are engaged in truth and merit—the earth milked by the sages.
Now therefore I shall explain how this earth was milked / long ago by the ancestors, O child, and by what rule:
Making a fine silver vessel, [they drew] the milk of the svadhā-offering accompanied by nectar; / appointing Yama as the calf, the milker was Antaka himself.
Then she was milked by the nāgas and serpents, [who made] Takṣaka the calf; / taking a bottle-gourd as the vessel, O best of the twice-born, venom was the milk.
The milker for the nāgas was the glorious Dhṛtarāṣṭra; / the serpents and nāgas, O best of the twice-born, subsist by that, peerless.
The nāgas also subsist on that extremely fierce, terrible venom, / O best of the twice-born, and so do the dread serpents.
By that very [milk] they subsist—the fierce, huge-bodied, mighty ones; / their food is of that nature, their conduct of that nature, their vigor and their valor of that nature.
Now therefore I shall explain how the earth was milked / by all the asuras and dānavas after assigning [the roles], O best of the twice-born.
The vessel in this case was an iron one, like a food-bowl, fulfilling all desires; / making the milk consist of māyā, which destroys all enemies.
Their calf was the glorious Virocana; / the two-headed priest of the daityas, Madhu of great strength, was the milker.
By that māyā, indeed, the daityas thrive—mighty, / possessing great intelligence, huge bodies, great splendor and valor.
That is their strength and their prowess; on that the dānavas live; / by that māyā even today, O best of the twice-born, they possess every illusion;
they thrive, endowed with measured wisdom; that is this strength of theirs. / In like manner was she milked by the yakṣas, that good earth, the support of all,
Thus we have heard, O chiefs of the vipras, from great-souled sages in a previous cosmic age: / there was milk full of disappearance in an extensive vessel of iron.
The very wise Vaiśravaṇa was then appointed as the calf— / the holy father of Maṇidhara, wise, the best among the intelligent.
And Rajatanābha, the wise one, was her milker— / all-knowing, knower of all dharma, the mighty son of the king of yakṣas,
eight-armed, of great splendor, two-headed, of great ascetic fervor; / on that too the yakṣas subsist at all times, O best of the twice-born.
Again, this earth was milked by the mighty rākṣasas, / and likewise by piśācas, who are tormented, having burned water,
[using] an upraised human skull, a vessel made of a corpse, [or] made of iron; / desiring to devour fine creatures, fierce in anger and valor.
Rajatanābha of great strength was their milker; / and Sumālin was the calf, and blood was the milk.
The rākṣasas, the yātudhānas, and the mighty piśācas, / and the yakṣas, live on that, as do the dread hosts of spirits.
The earth was milked again by the gandharvas and apsarases; / having made the very learned Citraratha the calf,
they milked in a lotus-vessel the gandharva [milk] consisting of song; / a gandharva named Suruci of great intellect was their [milker].
And he, most holy, was her milker, O best of the twice-born; / then the great-souled ones milked pure song as the excellent milk.
On that the gandharvas live, and likewise the other apsarases. / And this earth was milked by the highly sacred mountains,
[milking] various jewels and nectar-like herbs; / and the fortunate Himavat was appointed as the calf.
Meru became the milker, having made a rock-hewn vessel; / with that milk, all the mountains grew, possessing great power.
Again, she was milked by the great trees, the holy wish-fulfilling trees and others; / they brought a palāśa vessel, [milking] the sprouting [power] of what is cut down and burned.
The śāla tree, blossoming in its limbs, milked; the plakṣa tree became the calf then. / And then by the guhyakas, cāraṇas, siddhas, and troops of vidyādharas,
this supporter of all, granter of all desires, was milked; / whatever each group of beings desires, by means of specific vessels and calves,
she gives them milk of such a true nature through those respective means. / This is the supporter and the creator; this is the supreme earth,
the cow yielding all desires, adorned with sacred qualities; / this is the eldest, the foundation, this the creation, this the creatures,
the purifier, giver of merit, sacred, causing all crops to sprout, / the foundation and the source of all the moving and unmoving world.
This is Mahālakṣmī, this knowledge, always consisting of the entire universe, / milking all desires, the milker, sprouting all seeds,
the mother of all blessings, the bearer of all the worlds, / and the manifestation and form of the five gross elements.
Reaching to the ocean, this was known as Medinī, / being completely covered with the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Therefore, she is called Medinī by the proclaimers of the Veda. / Then, O best of men, because she surrendered to the wise Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
the goddess obtained the status of his daughter and is called Pṛthvī. / By that king, O best of twice-born, this earth was protected,
a foundation for villages and houses, garlanded with towns and cities, / rich with mines of grain, prosperous, and containing all sacred sites, O twice-born ones.
Thus the goddess Vasumatī is always composed of all worlds. / Such is the power of the king of kings as recounted in the Purāṇa.
The fortunate Pṛthu, son of Vena, brought all rites to light, / just like Viṣṇu, just like Brahmā, just like eternal Rudra.
The three gods are to be saluted by the gods and proclaimers of the Veda; / this best of kings is to be saluted by all brahmins and sages.
He who established the castes and life-stages, who upholds all the world, / is to be saluted by fortunate monarchs wishing for kingship in this world;
the primal king, the powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, is to be saluted / by warriors seeking mastery of the bow and always desiring victory.
The great king, giver of livelihood to the rulers of the earth, is to be saluted. / Thus, O best of twice-born, the particular vessels have been declared by me,
as well as the distinctive calves and the milkers before you, / and the distinction of the milk as ordained by the ruler of the earth.
It has been fully related to you accurately, as it was formerly: / auspicious, bringing renown, health, merit, and destroying sin.
Whoever hears the life of Pṛthu, son of Vena, O best of twice-born, / for him a bath in the Bhāgīrathī takes place day after day.
With his self cleansed of all sins, he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
